Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

zutable 0.0.0.9000

  • zutable_info() reports the package version.
  • Every condition the package raises inherits from zutable_error.
  • schema(), field() and not_null() describe a table’s columns with Arrow’s logical types: int32, float64, string, date, timestamp(unit, tz), decimal(p, s), enum(levels), list(type), struct(...) and more, read inside the call so they mask nothing. schema() of a data frame infers its types.
  • A POSIXct with no time zone is typed timestamp("us", "UTC").
  • na(type) gives a typed missing value, for placeholders.
  • register_extension_type() lets a package type its vector class as an Arrow extension.
  • zutable() and as_zutable() create typed tables: plain data frames that carry their schema and print it under the column names. Values enter exactly or not at all.
  • conform() checks a table against a schema and lists every mismatch; metadata() returns a table’s key-value pairs.
  • Base R’s value forms (x[i, ], x[, j], x$col) work, so head(), subset(), split() and unique() return zutables. No replacement changes a table’s schema: a value must fit its column’s type, and renaming or removing a column is an error.
  • Expressions are written in a closed, typed vocabulary of SQL-named functions with R synonyms (?vocabulary): arithmetic, comparison, logic, strings, patterns, dates, cast(), case(), aggregates, and r() to run arbitrary R. Every expression is typed before any data is read, and every function gives the same result locally and in DuckDB.
  • The bracket takes SQL’s clauses as named arguments: where, select (with .all and -name), order (with desc()), limit and distinct, run in SQL’s logical order. x[cond, .(...)] reads as in data.table, and a position that mentions no column is a value form.
  • explain() prints the plan that made a table, one step per line; dplyr::explain() reaches it too.
  • by, having and the aggregates (count(), sum(), mean(), min(), max(), first(), last(), any(), all(), count_distinct()) make aggregate queries; groups come in order of first appearance and NA is a group. over(aggregate, by = ) computes an aggregate per partition without collapsing rows.
  • x[, col := value] and blocks x[, { a := ...; b <- ...; c := ... }] update existing columns in place, keeping their types, with where and by; a block is typed as a whole and committed at once. copy() gives an independent table; freeze() marks a table so that nothing writes to it again.
  • join() matches two tables on keys of the same type (inner, left, right, full, semi and anti), with multiple for fan-out, na_equal for missing keys and suffix for clashing names; rbind() stacks tables of identical schemas.
  • .col(name) refers to a column whose name is held in a variable.
  • zutable_info() reports the kernel header’s version and the zufast headers the package was built against; the header zutable.h is installed for other packages to use through LinkingTo.
  • grp() groups rows by keys of any kind (integer, double, logical, character, factor, integer64, raw), in first-appearance or key order; the bracket’s by runs on it. It is a hash table of five bytes a slot, partitioned to the cache above L3.
  • key_order() gives the stable permutation that sorts rows by one or more keys, and key_rank() their ranks, as order(method = "radix") and rank() do, with decreasing per key and na.last. They run the kernel’s hybrid sort: Vergesort’s run detection in front of counting sort, pdqsort, LSD radix and ska sort, chosen by size and key width. The bracket’s order and grp(sort = TRUE) run on it.
  • grp(sort = TRUE) sorts every row instead of hashing when that is faster: below a million rows, and above when about 1% of the rows or more are distinct keys. The result is the same either way.
  • key_order() and key_rank() sort strings in the kernel, by the bytes of their UTF-8 text, and with collate = TRUE in the locale’s order through stringi (a Suggests), whose collation keys are computed once per distinct string; without stringi, collate = TRUE is a zutable_collate_error.
  • key_sort() sorts values, as sort(method = "radix") does, and the result remembers that it is sorted and whether it holds NA, so a later sort(), is.unsorted() or anyNA() answers without a pass; modifying it in place forgets both. grp(sort = TRUE)’s first key column carries the same.
  • grp_join() returns the index pairs of an inner, left, semi or anti join on one or several keys, in x’s row order and then y’s, with multiple to keep every match, the first, the last, or to raise a zutable_multiple_error; grp_match() generalises match() to several keys. join() now runs on them.
  • join(how = "right", multiple = "error") counts the rows of x that match each row of y, as documented; it used to raise on a row of x matching several rows of y. The error names the side its row is in.
  • grp_reduce() computes sum, prod, mean, min, max, count, nobs, first and last by group in one pass, several columns at once, with na.rm and a broadcast back to the rows ("replace", "subtract", "divide"). Sums and means are base R’s bit for bit; a group with no values left is NA.
  • The bracket’s aggregates, over() and := with by now reduce every group at once through grp_reduce()’s kernel, rather than evaluating each group in turn: 8 to 130 times faster at 10^6 rows, with the same results.
  • The kernel’s header, <zutable.h>, is usable from another package’s C with LinkingTo: zutable alone, as a test package shows on every OS. The accumulators a caller passes to zt_reduce() must be aligned for zt_acc (16 bytes on x86_64, beyond what R_alloc() promises).
